implementation_notes: The .NET BCL exposes no managed prefetch API; the surface is System.Runtime.Intrinsics.X86.Sse.Prefetch0/1/2 (and X86Base.Prefetch0) plus, in .NET 9+, Sse.PrefetchNonTemporal, guarded by IsSupported so the code degrades gracefully. This is genuinely a different ergonomics story from C/C++: the JIT's own memory model handles most latency, and a managed prefetch can be removed or reordered by the JIT because the platform only promises a hint. For the OS-level analogue, P/Invoke to posix_fadvise or a FileStream with a SequentialScan option is the practical answer for file readahead; and for managed heaps the equivalent of prefetching is ensuring locality by layout, not by hint. Measure with dotnet-counters before adding anything: on a managed runtime the miss is often in the GC layout, not the prefetch.
idiom_name: System.Runtime.Intrinsics X86 Sse.Prefetch0/1/2 (SSE4.1) guarded by IsSupported; or layout-based locality
pitfalls: Sse.Prefetch* requires SSE support (x86 with SSE4.1); the intrinsic must be guarded by IsSupported or it is a no-op or throws on some runtimes.
The JIT may treat the prefetch as a hint and reorder or drop it, so a managed prefetch is weaker-guaranteed than the intrinsic in native code.
On a managed heap, the dominant miss is often the object's placement, not the array load - fixing layout (structs, arrays of structs) usually beats hinting.
FileOptions.SequentialScan is the practical readahead lever and is frequently the highest-ratio prefetch win available in a managed service.
